./framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review.md:16:**What it is** — A minimal written record Weber attaches to the end of every decision-oriented meeting format in the course: the action taken, who owns it, the due date, and the review method and date (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 04:48–05:56). The same four fields recur, worded slightly differently, in every later meeting format, per the lesson summaries: the meeting-typology **decide** mode requires an explicit decision, owner, due date, and review (Lab 3B summary, 01:03–02:14); stoplight storytelling ends with one owner, one action, a due date, and a review point recorded in the decision log (Lab 3C summary, 03:02–03:45); and the 20-minutes-of-discipline format ends with the decision, actions, accountable people, deadlines, and a requested update (Podcast 3 summary, 08:34–09:39).
./framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review.md:18:**Why it works** — Weber's stated rationale, per the lesson summary, is that the administrative effort of writing the four fields down creates accountability and reduces later disagreement about what was agreed (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 04:48–05:56). **Inference:** without a record, a verbal decision is likely subject to selective memory once circumstances change or the outcome is unwelcome; the log exists specifically to prevent that after-the-fact renegotiation.
./framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure.md:16:**What it is** — Weber's structured meeting format for use when the question and realistic options are already clear and the team needs to decide, not explore. Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).
./framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure.md:18:**Why it works** — Weber's own stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 00:00–02:18). **Inference:** forcing preparation and concise contributions likely works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.
./framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure.md:20:**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone, aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).

Elements: prepare before the meeting by defining the question and narrowing it to two or three realistic options, with relevant information available in advance so participants arrive informed; keep evidence precise, stating what was measured, what is known, and what remains unknown; time-box contributions so short speaking limits push people to the critical information, with supporting detail left in the pre-read; and leave a decision log recording the action, owner, due date, and review method (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 00:00–05:56; see [[framework--decision-log-owner-action-date-review]]). Brainstorming, complex technical work, and staff development are explicitly carved out as needing a different, slower pace (05:56–07:27).
./framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure.md:18:**Why it works** — Weber's own stated priority for this format is speed, clarity, and accountability specifically when the decision space is already narrow (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 00:00–02:18). **Inference:** forcing preparation and concise contributions likely works because the hard thinking (narrowing the options, gathering the evidence) has already happened before the room convenes, so meeting time is spent deciding, not discovering.
./framework--kaigi-decision-meeting-structure.md:20:**When to apply** — Recurring operational decisions with a known, bounded option set: Weber's own worked example is an AFL pre-training Go/No-Go review, where a leader names each player, responsible practitioners give concise observations, other staff add relevant information without repeated prompting, and the group combines evidence rather than changing training on one measure alone, aiming for under 30 seconds per player across roughly 50 players, with flagged players receiving assigned follow-up reported back within 20 minutes (Lab 3A summary (Kaigi-summary.md), 07:28–12:13). Weber also shows the format can be dropped into a stalled meeting mid-stream: switch explicitly into a 10-minute decision phase, state the decision, establish ownership, document the outcome, and move on (12:14–13:23).
